summary: An announcement that UCSB now ran a server program supporting part of the Remote Job Entry protocol of RFC 407, reachable at a particular socket. It explains the login details and the transmission mode available at the time. More detailed documentation was promised in a later RFC.

plainLanguage.summary: UCSB announces a server that accepts remote job-entry requests. The note explains how users sign in and warns that only part of the protocol is supported.

what socket did the ucsb rjs server use
subtitle: A notice that UCSB offered a server for basic Remote Job Entry operations.

tldr.problem: Users needed to know that UCSB offered a Remote Job Entry server and how to access its supported functions.
tldr.mechanism: The server is available under socket 5 and supports a subset of the Remote Job Entry Protocol described in RFC 407.
tldr.outcome: The announcement describes login, supported modes, account commands, and features not yet implemented; fuller documentation was promised.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 436 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. The text announces a site-specific service and describes its early limits.

sections.title: The UCSB RJS Server
sections.content:
Mark Krilanovich announces that a server program is resident under socket 5 at UCSB. It supports a subset of the Remote Job Entry Protocol in RFC 407, and the RFC gives enough information to use basic functions.

The author says a more detailed document will follow.
sections.plainLanguage: The notice identifies where the service listens and which protocol it partly supports. It introduces the basic way to use the service.

sections.title: Logging In
sections.content:
Users log in with a user ID and password, each containing one to eight alphanumeric characters, with a letter first. A user ID is arbitrary at this stage; the first password used with that ID becomes the password required for later logins.

The RFC says UCSB Computer Center would eventually assign user ID and password pairs.
sections.plainLanguage: A user chooses an ID and password initially and must use that password again with the same ID. The note says assigned pairs were planned for later.

sections.title: Supported Features
sections.content:
The server supports transmission mode T; other modes are treated as T. It supports the default transmit-and-discard disposition, and the note lists commands such as ABORT, ALTER, RESTART, and SKIP as not yet implemented.

It also documents account commands for users of TENEX FTP servers and gives shortcuts for some other commands.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a limited set of functions works at this stage. The RFC lists unfinished commands and explains a few account-related options.
